title: Given a singly linked list, reverse its nodes k at a time and return the modified list, leaving any trailing group of fewer than k nodes in original order.
shortTitle: Reverse Nodes in a Linked List in Groups of k

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing a linked list in groups of k processes the list in consecutive blocks of k nodes, reversing the pointers within each full block while leaving a final block of fewer than k nodes untouched. The standard approach walks the list, and for each block it first confirms k nodes remain, then reverses that block in place and reconnects it to the previously reversed portion and to the rest. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India processes a chain of transaction records and must flip the order of every fixed-size batch, say every three records, to match a downstream system's expectation, but if the last batch is short it must be left as it is. A clerk looks ahead to confirm she has a full batch of three; if so she reverses just those three in place and stitches the reversed batch onto what she has already done, then moves to the next batch. When fewer than three records remain at the end, she leaves them exactly as they are and stops.
s1_definition.oneliner: Check that k nodes remain, reverse that block in place, reconnect it, then repeat; leave a short final block alone.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing a linked list in groups of k processes the list in consecutive blocks of k nodes, reversing the pointers within each full block while leaving a final block of fewer than k nodes untouched. The standard approach walks the list, and for each block it first confirms k nodes remain, then reverses that block in place and reconnects it to the previously reversed portion and to the rest. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India processes a chain of transaction records and must flip the order of every fixed-size batch, say every three records, to match a downstream system's expectation, but if the last batch is short it must be left as it is. A clerk looks ahead to confirm she has a full batch of three; if so she reverses just those three in place and stitches the reversed batch onto what she has already done, then moves to the next batch. When fewer than three records remain at the end, she leaves them exactly as they are and stops.

**One line to remember:** Check that k nodes remain, reverse that block in place, reconnect it, then repeat; leave a short final block alone.

sections.s2_technical:
This problem combines two skills: reversing a singly linked list, and carefully stitching reversed segments back together without losing any nodes. The stitching is where most bugs live, so a dummy head node that sits before the real head simplifies the reconnection enormously, because it gives you a stable handle to the node that precedes the current group.

The driver keeps a pointer to the node just before the current group, starting at the dummy. For each group it first walks k steps ahead to verify a full group of k nodes exists; if fewer than k remain, it stops and leaves the tail as is. If a full group exists, it reverses exactly those k nodes using the standard previous-current-next reversal, iterating k times and flipping each node's next pointer to its predecessor. After reversing, three reconnections are needed: the node before the group must now point to the new front of the reversed group, the original first node of the group, which is now the group's tail, must point to the node that follows the group, and you advance the before-group pointer to that original first node to prepare for the next group.

The key invariants are not losing the pointer to the rest of the list and reconnecting in the right order. A common pattern captures the group's start and the node after the group before reversing, reverses, then wires up the three links. Because each node is visited a constant number of times, once to check the group boundary and once to reverse, the total work is linear, and because only a handful of pointers are used, the space is constant.

A senior-level nuance is the recursive formulation and real applications. Recursively, you reverse the first k nodes and set the original first node's next to the result of recursing on the rest, which is elegant but uses stack space proportional to the number of groups, so the iterative version is preferred for very long lists. The partial-last-group rule is a deliberate specification detail that tests whether you read requirements carefully, and the general technique of reversing and re-linking sublists appears in batch reordering, pagination of linked structures, and buffer manipulation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India feeds transaction records as a linked chain to a downstream settlement system that expects each fixed-size batch in reversed order, while any leftover partial batch at the end must be passed through unchanged. This is exactly reversing a linked list in groups of k.

Problem 2 — The reversal must happen in place on a potentially very long chain without allocating a parallel structure, and no record may be lost or duplicated during the pointer surgery. Using a dummy head and reconnecting the three links carefully guarantees integrity in constant space.

In our mini-project we build a `BatchReverser` over a linked node of transaction IDs with a `reverseInGroups` method. The demo reverses a five-node chain in groups of two, leaving the final single node in place, and logs the resulting order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the chain T1 to T2 to T3 to T4 to T5, reversing in groups of two.

Step 1: A dummy node sits before T1, and the before-group pointer starts at the dummy. We check whether two nodes remain from T1; T1 and T2 exist, so we have a full group.

Step 2: Reverse the first group of two. Flipping pointers turns T1 to T2 into T2 to T1. The original first node T1 becomes the group's tail. We reconnect: the dummy now points to T2, the new front, and T1's next will be wired to the rest in the next move.

Step 3: Wire T1's next to the node after the group, which is T3, and advance the before-group pointer to T1, the group's tail, ready for the next group. The chain so far reads T2, T1, then T3 onward.

Step 4: Check whether two nodes remain from T3; T3 and T4 exist, so another full group. Reverse T3 to T4 into T4 to T3. Reconnect: T1 now points to T4, the new front, and T3, now the group tail, points to T5, the rest. Advance the before-group pointer to T3.

Step 5: Check whether two nodes remain from T5; only T5 exists, which is fewer than two, so we stop and leave T5 in place.

Step 6: The final chain reads T2, T1, T4, T3, T5. Each full group of two was reversed in place, the trailing single node was left unchanged per the specification, and no node was lost or duplicated during the pointer surgery.

```
[2026-10-26 23:44:01] INFO    Reordered chain: T2 → T1 → T4 → T3 → T5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  input:  T1 → T2 → T3 → T4 → T5      k=2
  dummy → T1 ...

  group1 [T1,T2] full → reverse → T2 → T1
     dummy→T2, T1→(rest)
  group2 [T3,T4] full → reverse → T4 → T3
     T1→T4, T3→T5
  group3 [T5]   partial (<k) → leave as is

  output: T2 → T1 → T4 → T3 → T5
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a linked list in groups of k means processing the list in consecutive blocks of k nodes, reversing the pointers within each full block, and leaving any final block of fewer than k nodes in its original order. It combines two skills, reversing a singly linked list and carefully stitching the reversed segments back together, and the stitching is where the bugs live, so I always use a dummy head node that sits before the real head to give me a stable handle on the node preceding each group.

My driver keeps a pointer to the node just before the current group, starting at the dummy. For each group I first walk k steps ahead to confirm a full group of k nodes exists, and if fewer than k remain I stop and leave the tail unchanged. For a full group I reverse exactly those k nodes with the standard previous-current-next reversal, flipping each node's next pointer to its predecessor, then I make three reconnections: the node before the group points to the new front of the reversed block, the original first node of the group, now the block's tail, points to the node after the group, and I advance the before-group pointer to that original first node for the next iteration. Because each node is touched a constant number of times and I use only a few pointers, the algorithm is linear time and constant space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to feed transaction records to a settlement system that expects each fixed-size batch in reversed order while passing any leftover partial batch through unchanged. The reversal happened in place on very long chains without allocating a parallel structure, and the dummy head plus careful three-link reconnection guaranteed no record was lost or duplicated during the pointer surgery.

The senior-level point I make is the recursive alternative and the specification detail. Recursively I would reverse the first k nodes and set the original first node's next to the result of recursing on the rest, which is elegant but uses stack space proportional to the number of groups, so I prefer the iterative version for very long lists. I also highlight that the leave-the-partial-tail rule is a deliberate requirement that tests whether I read the specification carefully, and that the broader technique of reversing and re-linking sublists shows up in batch reordering, pagination of linked structures, and buffer manipulation.
